questions.question_text: Which statement best describes family assessment in midwifery practice?

choices.text: A systematic collection of information about family structure, relationships, health needs and available resources
An examination of the pregnant woman without considering her home environment
A process of identifying only the family's financial difficulties
A procedure used exclusively when a woman develops obstetric complications

questions.rationale: Family assessment is a systematic process of identifying the health needs, strengths, relationships and resources of a family. It helps the midwife plan care that considers the woman within her family and social environment.

questions.question_text: A midwife is assessing a pregnant woman who lives with her husband, children, mother-in-law and husband's younger siblings. Which family structure is being described?

choices.text: Nuclear family
Extended family
Single-parent family
Child-headed household

questions.rationale: An extended family includes relatives beyond the parents and their children, such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and siblings. This structure is common in Ghana and may influence decision-making and support during pregnancy.

questions.question_text: During antenatal assessment, a woman reports that her husband's relatives make most decisions about her healthcare. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Accept the relatives' decisions as final because they are senior family members
Ask the woman privately about her preferences, safety and decision-making needs
Instruct the woman to leave her husband's family immediately
Refuse to provide further antenatal care until the family changes its behaviour

questions.rationale: The midwife should establish the woman's own wishes and assess whether she is experiencing coercion or restricted autonomy. Respectful, confidential communication helps protect her rights while allowing appropriate family involvement with her consent.

questions.question_text: Which information is most important when assessing the support available to a pregnant woman?

choices.text: The number of television sets in the household
The occupations of all neighbours
Who can provide transport, emotional support and assistance during emergencies
The family's preferred type of entertainment

questions.rationale: Practical and emotional support can influence whether a woman attends antenatal care, follows a birth plan and reaches a health facility promptly. Identifying available support also helps the midwife address gaps before complications occur.

questions.question_text: A woman attending antenatal clinic has a history of hypertension in her mother and sister. Why should the midwife document this information?

choices.text: It establishes that the woman will definitely develop hypertension
It provides relevant family history that may help identify health risks and guide assessment
It removes the need to monitor the woman's blood pressure
It confirms that her relatives must attend every antenatal appointment

questions.rationale: Family history can reveal inherited or shared risk factors that may be relevant to maternal health. It supports risk assessment but does not establish that the woman will necessarily develop the condition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key purpose of assessing family strengths during pregnancy?

choices.text: To identify resources that can support healthy maternal and newborn outcomes
To determine which family member should control the woman's healthcare
To replace clinical assessment with family opinions
To identify reasons for excluding relatives from maternity care

questions.rationale: A strengths-based assessment identifies existing abilities, relationships and resources that can support the woman. It avoids focusing only on problems and helps the midwife develop realistic care plans with the family.

questions.question_text: A pregnant adolescent lives with her aunt, who provides most of her daily care. Her biological parents live elsewhere. Which issue should the midwife particularly clarify during family assessment?

choices.text: Whether the aunt has the same occupation as the adolescent's parents
The adolescent's favourite household activities
The adolescent's support system, safeguarding needs and appropriate consent arrangements
Whether the aunt can independently change all clinical decisions

questions.rationale: Kinship care occurs when relatives such as aunts, grandparents or other family members provide care for a child. The midwife should assess the adolescent's safety, support and legal consent requirements while respecting her confidentiality and evolving capacity.

questions.question_text: Which communication technique involves allowing a client to express feelings without interruption or premature judgement?

choices.text: Confrontation
Active listening
False reassurance
Changing the subject

questions.rationale: Active listening involves giving full attention to the speaker and responding in a way that demonstrates understanding. It helps establish trust and encourages the woman to share concerns relevant to her care.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman tells the midwife, 'I am afraid I may die during childbirth.' Which response is most therapeutic?

choices.text: Do not think about death; childbirth is always safe
Other women have given birth, so you should not worry
Can you tell me more about what makes you afraid?
You should stop listening to frightening stories from people

questions.rationale: An open-ended question encourages the woman to explain the source of her fear. This allows the midwife to assess her concerns, provide accurate information and offer appropriate emotional support.

questions.question_text: During counselling, a woman becomes tearful after discussing a previous stillbirth. What is the most appropriate initial response by the midwife?

choices.text: Immediately change the topic to avoid upsetting her
Allow her time, remain present and acknowledge her feelings
Tell her that she must be strong for her current pregnancy
Explain that previous pregnancy losses should be forgotten

questions.rationale: Remaining present and acknowledging the woman's feelings demonstrates empathy and emotional support. The midwife should allow her to express grief without minimising the experience or forcing her to discuss more than she wishes.

questions.question_text: Which statement is an example of an open-ended question during antenatal counselling?

choices.text: Have you attended antenatal clinic before?
Are you taking your prescribed medication?
Do you have a husband?
How has your family responded to your pregnancy?

questions.rationale: Open-ended questions encourage detailed responses rather than simple yes-or-no answers. They help the midwife understand the woman's experiences, relationships and concerns.

questions.question_text: A woman with limited formal education does not understand the midwife's explanation of danger signs in pregnancy. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Repeat the same technical explanation more loudly
Use simple language, appropriate local-language communication and teach-back
Ask her husband to explain everything without involving her
Assume she understands because she remained silent

questions.rationale: Health information should be communicated in language and terms the woman can understand. Teach-back allows the midwife to check comprehension by asking the woman to explain the information in her own words.

questions.question_text: A woman discloses during a private consultation that her partner physically assaults her. What is the midwife's priority response?

choices.text: Confront the partner immediately without discussing safety with the woman
Advise her to tolerate the violence to preserve the marriage
Listen without judgement, assess immediate safety and explain available support and referral options
Share the disclosure with other patients to obtain their opinions

questions.rationale: The midwife should respond confidentially and non-judgementally while assessing immediate danger and the woman's safety needs. Appropriate referral and safeguarding procedures should be followed, with disclosure limited to what is necessary and legally required.

questions.question_text: Which action is most likely to interfere with therapeutic communication between a midwife and a pregnant woman?

choices.text: Maintaining appropriate eye contact according to cultural preferences
Using medical jargon that the woman does not understand
Allowing the woman to ask questions
Clarifying information before making assumptions

questions.rationale: Unexplained medical terminology can create confusion and prevent the woman from participating meaningfully in decisions. The midwife should use clear language and confirm understanding.

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of a genogram in family assessment?

choices.text: To illustrate family structure, relationships and relevant health history across generations
To measure the distance between a home and a health facility
To record only the family's monthly income
To determine the exact date of delivery

questions.rationale: A genogram is a diagrammatic representation of family relationships and structure across generations. It can also document relevant health conditions and relationship patterns that may influence maternity care.

questions.question_text: A midwife wants to identify a pregnant woman's connections with her church, workplace, health facility and extended family. Which assessment tool is most appropriate?

choices.text: Partograph
Ecomap
Growth chart
Medication chart

questions.rationale: An ecomap illustrates the relationships and connections between a family and external systems in its environment. It helps identify supportive relationships, stressful connections and gaps in social support.

questions.question_text: In a genogram, why is it important to include information about a history of multiple births and inherited conditions where relevant?

choices.text: To predict the exact outcome of every future pregnancy
To replace antenatal investigations
To identify family patterns that may require further clinical assessment or counselling
To determine which relative should supervise the midwife

questions.rationale: A genogram can help identify patterns of inherited conditions and reproductive history across generations. Such findings may guide further assessment, counselling or referral but cannot independently establish a diagnosis.

questions.question_text: An ecomap shows that a pregnant woman has strong support from her mother and church but experiences conflict with her partner and has difficulty accessing transport. What should the midwife conclude?

choices.text: The woman has no social support because her partner is not supportive
The woman has both protective support systems and important barriers requiring intervention
The church should take responsibility for all clinical decisions
The transport problem is unrelated to maternity care

questions.rationale: An ecomap identifies both supportive and stressful relationships within a woman's social environment. The midwife can build on existing support while developing a realistic transport and safety plan.

questions.question_text: What is patient advocacy in midwifery?

choices.text: Making every healthcare decision on behalf of the woman
Supporting and protecting the woman's rights, preferences, dignity and access to appropriate care
Allowing family members to override the woman's decisions
Providing care only when the woman agrees with the midwife

questions.rationale: Patient advocacy involves protecting the woman's rights and supporting her informed participation in healthcare decisions. It includes promoting dignity, privacy, informed consent and access to appropriate services.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour refuses a vaginal examination after the midwife explains its purpose. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Proceed because the examination is part of routine maternity care
Ask the woman's relatives to force her to accept the examination
Respect her decision, explore her concerns and explain alternative ways of monitoring where appropriate
Discharge her immediately for refusing care

questions.rationale: A competent woman has the right to accept or refuse an examination after receiving relevant information. The midwife should explore her concerns, explain the implications and continue appropriate care while documenting the discussion.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman who is eligible for NHIS benefits is told that she cannot receive an essential maternity service until she pays an unofficial fee. What is the midwife's most appropriate action?

choices.text: Ignore the matter because payment issues are not related to patient advocacy
Advise her to abandon antenatal care
Clarify her entitlement and help her access the appropriate facility channels for resolving the issue
Pay the fee personally and make no report of the incident

questions.rationale: Advocacy includes helping women navigate barriers to accessing entitled healthcare services. The midwife should clarify applicable NHIS coverage and follow facility procedures to address inappropriate charges without making unsupported promises about coverage.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe vaginal bleeding after delivery is waiting because her relatives insist that a traditional healer should examine her first. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Wait until the family completes its preferred traditional treatment
Prioritise emergency assessment and stabilisation, explain the danger and involve the family without delaying urgent care
Discharge the woman because the family disagrees with the facility
Allow the relatives to decide whether the bleeding is serious

questions.rationale: Severe postpartum bleeding is a life-threatening obstetric emergency requiring immediate assessment, resuscitation and escalation. Cultural concerns should be addressed respectfully, but urgent life-saving care must not be delayed.

questions.question_text: Which action best demonstrates respect for informed consent during maternity care?

choices.text: Explaining the proposed procedure, its benefits, material risks and alternatives before obtaining voluntary agreement
Obtaining consent only from the woman's husband
Asking the woman to sign a form without explaining the procedure
Assuming consent because the woman attended the health facility

questions.rationale: Informed consent requires understandable information, voluntariness and agreement from the woman who has decision-making capacity. A signature alone does not replace meaningful explanation and an opportunity to ask questions.

questions.question_text: A woman requests privacy during labour, but several relatives insist on remaining in the delivery room. Which response by the midwife best supports the woman's rights?

choices.text: Allow all relatives to remain because family involvement is always beneficial
Ask the husband to make the final decision about who stays
Explain that the woman's preference for privacy should guide who is present, subject to safety and facility requirements
Refuse to provide care until the family leaves the facility

questions.rationale: The woman has a right to privacy and should be involved in decisions about who is present during her care. The midwife should communicate this respectfully while maintaining appropriate clinical and infection-prevention requirements.

questions.question_text: What is a major purpose of a home visit by a midwife during pregnancy?

choices.text: To replace all scheduled antenatal clinic visits
To assess the woman's home circumstances, identify needs and provide appropriate support or referral
To inspect the household for unrelated legal violations
To allow relatives to make clinical decisions without the woman

questions.rationale: A home visit allows the midwife to understand the woman's living conditions, support systems and possible barriers to care. It complements, rather than replaces, facility-based antenatal assessment and other required clinical services.

questions.question_text: Before conducting a routine home visit to a pregnant woman, which action should the midwife take?

choices.text: Visit without identifying herself or explaining the purpose
Obtain or confirm the woman's agreement, plan the visit and review relevant information
Inform every neighbour about the woman's pregnancy
Ask the family to conduct the clinical assessment before arrival

questions.rationale: Preparation includes confirming the visit, clarifying its purpose and reviewing relevant information to ensure that the visit is useful and safe. Respecting consent and confidentiality is essential when providing care in the home.

questions.question_text: During a home visit, a pregnant woman at 34 weeks reports severe headache and blurred vision. What is the midwife's priority action?

choices.text: Advise her to rest and reassess her symptoms at the next scheduled visit
Recommend herbal treatment for the headache
Arrange urgent assessment at an appropriate health facility because of possible severe pre-eclampsia
Ask her to increase her daily water intake and remain at home

questions.rationale: Severe headache and visual disturbance in pregnancy are danger signs that may indicate severe pre-eclampsia. The woman requires urgent clinical assessment and appropriate referral rather than routine follow-up at home.

questions.question_text: A midwife notices during a home visit that a pregnant woman has no reliable transport to the nearest health facility. Which intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Document the barrier and work with the woman and available support systems to develop an emergency transport plan
Tell her that transport arrangements are entirely her responsibility
Advise her to deliver at home regardless of her risk status
Wait until labour begins before discussing transport

questions.rationale: A birth preparedness and complication readiness plan should address transport and access to emergency obstetric care. Involving trusted relatives and community resources can reduce delays in reaching a facility.

questions.question_text: During a home visit, a midwife finds that a woman who recently delivered has heavy vaginal bleeding, dizziness and cold clammy skin. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Complete the routine home-visit checklist before taking action
Recognise a possible postpartum haemorrhage, activate emergency assistance and arrange urgent transfer while initiating appropriate immediate care
Advise the woman to sleep and return the following day
Ask the family to prepare a traditional herbal drink

questions.rationale: Heavy bleeding with signs of circulatory compromise suggests a potentially life-threatening postpartum haemorrhage. Emergency assistance, immediate management within the midwife's competence and urgent transfer are priorities.

questions.question_text: Which observation during a home visit is most relevant to assessing the newborn's immediate home environment?

choices.text: The family's preferred television programme
The colour of the household furniture
The availability of a clean sleeping area, warmth and safe newborn-care practices
The number of visitors who attended the naming ceremony

questions.rationale: A safe newborn environment includes appropriate warmth, hygiene and safe sleeping arrangements. Assessing these factors allows the midwife to identify risks and provide practical health education.

questions.question_text: A midwife visits a pregnant woman whose family refuses to allow her to speak privately. The woman appears frightened and avoids answering questions. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Continue asking sensitive questions in front of the family
Respectfully seek an opportunity to speak with the woman privately and assess her safety
Assume that the family is supportive because they are present
End all contact with the woman permanently

questions.rationale: A private conversation may be necessary to assess the woman's autonomy, safety and possible exposure to coercion or abuse. The midwife should avoid actions that could increase risk and follow appropriate safeguarding and referral procedures.

questions.question_text: Which principle is central to family-centred maternity care?

choices.text: The family should make all decisions regardless of the woman's wishes
Care should respect the woman's preferences while involving supportive family members with her consent
All women should receive identical care without considering individual needs
Family members should replace trained health professionals during childbirth

questions.rationale: Family-centred maternity care recognises the importance of the woman's relationships and support systems while maintaining her autonomy. Family participation should be guided by the woman's preferences and informed consent.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour requests that her sister provide emotional support during childbirth. The sister meets facility requirements and the woman continues to want her present. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Permit the sister's presence in accordance with the woman's preference and facility safety requirements
Insist that only the husband can provide birth companionship
Refuse because relatives have no role in maternity care
Allow the sister to perform clinical procedures during labour

questions.rationale: A chosen birth companion can provide emotional reassurance and support during labour. The woman's preference should guide the choice, while clinical responsibilities remain with qualified healthcare professionals.

questions.question_text: A couple attends antenatal education together. Which outcome best demonstrates effective family-centred education?

choices.text: The partner makes all decisions about the woman's delivery
The woman and her partner understand danger signs, birth preparedness and how to seek emergency care
The partner receives information while the woman remains excluded
The couple agrees to avoid facility care unless complications become severe

questions.rationale: Effective antenatal education equips the woman and her chosen support person with knowledge to recognise danger signs and respond appropriately. It strengthens preparedness without transferring the woman's decision-making authority to her partner.

questions.question_text: A woman has an uncomplicated vaginal birth and wishes to begin breastfeeding immediately. Her relatives request that the newborn be taken away for a traditional ceremony first. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Delay breastfeeding until the relatives complete the ceremony
Explain the benefits of early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding, support the woman's choice and discuss safe ways to accommodate cultural practices
Allow relatives to decide when breastfeeding should begin
Separate the newborn from the mother for the remainder of the day

questions.rationale: Early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding support newborn thermal regulation, bonding and successful breastfeeding. The midwife should respectfully discuss cultural practices while protecting essential newborn care and the mother's preferences.

questions.question_text: Which action best promotes continuity of family-centred maternity care after childbirth?

choices.text: Providing discharge information only to the relatives
Ending communication with the family once the woman leaves the maternity unit
Arranging appropriate postnatal follow-up and involving the woman and her chosen support person in newborn-care education
Advising the family to seek professional care only when the newborn becomes seriously ill

questions.rationale: Continuity of care connects facility-based maternity services with postnatal follow-up and newborn health services. Education should involve the woman and any support person she chooses, while ensuring that the mother remains central to care decisions.

questions.question_text: A woman with a high-risk pregnancy wishes to involve her mother in discussions about her birth plan. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Exclude the mother because high-risk care must always be discussed with the woman alone
Invite the mother to participate with the woman's consent while ensuring that clinical decisions remain informed and the woman's preferences are respected
Allow the mother to consent to all procedures on behalf of the woman
Ask the mother to choose the delivery method without consulting the woman

questions.rationale: Family involvement can strengthen support and shared understanding when the woman wants it. However, the woman remains the primary decision-maker when she has capacity to make her own healthcare decisions.

questions.question_text: What is culturally sensitive maternity care?

choices.text: Providing care that respects cultural beliefs and practices while maintaining safety, dignity and evidence-based standards
Accepting every cultural practice even when it causes serious harm
Providing maternity care only according to the midwife's personal beliefs
Avoiding discussion of cultural beliefs during antenatal care

questions.rationale: Culturally sensitive care recognises that beliefs and traditions influence pregnancy and childbirth experiences. The midwife should respect cultural identity while explaining and addressing practices that may create health risks.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman explains that her family expects her to avoid eating certain nutritious foods during pregnancy because they believe these foods will make the baby too large. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Ridicule the belief and tell her that her family is ignorant
Explore the belief respectfully and provide accurate nutrition information using culturally appropriate examples
Tell her to follow the restriction without assessing its nutritional consequences
Advise her to stop eating all foods prepared by relatives

questions.rationale: The midwife should understand the belief before providing appropriate nutrition counselling. Respectful education can correct misconceptions while helping the woman maintain an adequate and balanced diet.

questions.question_text: A woman requests that a trusted female relative be present during labour because of her cultural and personal preferences. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Dismiss the request because cultural preferences are not relevant to clinical care
Assess the request and facilitate it where possible, with the woman's consent and in accordance with safety requirements
Allow the relative to make all clinical decisions
Tell the woman that she must accept whichever companion the facility chooses

questions.rationale: Respecting the woman's preferred support person can improve comfort and promote a positive childbirth experience. The midwife should facilitate the request when it is compatible with the woman's wishes and safe facility practice.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour requests to adopt an upright position, but a relative insists that she must lie flat because this is the family's tradition. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Follow the relative's instruction without consulting the woman
Explain safe labour-position options and support the woman's informed preference when clinically appropriate
Force the woman to remain in the supine position throughout labour
Ask the relative to conduct the delivery

questions.rationale: Women should be supported to use comfortable and appropriate positions during labour when there is no clinical contraindication. The midwife should communicate respectfully with relatives while ensuring that the woman's preferences remain central.

questions.question_text: A family wishes to apply an unsterile substance to the umbilical stump of a newborn as part of a traditional practice. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Allow the practice because all traditional newborn-care practices are harmless
Explain the risk of infection and recommend clean, dry cord care in accordance with newborn-care guidance
Advise the family to cover the stump tightly with a dirty cloth
Avoid discussing the practice because it may offend the family

questions.rationale: Applying unsterile substances to the umbilical stump can introduce infection and increase the risk of neonatal sepsis. The midwife should explain the risk respectfully and promote recommended clean, dry cord care.

questions.question_text: During labour, a woman's relatives insist that she should not receive pain relief because childbirth pain is traditionally considered necessary. The woman privately requests information about available pain-relief options. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Follow the relatives' preference because they represent the family
Provide balanced information privately and support the woman's informed decision about appropriate pain relief
Tell the woman that pain relief is never appropriate during childbirth
Ask the relatives to approve every clinical intervention

questions.rationale: The woman has the right to receive information and make informed decisions about her care. Cultural beliefs should be approached respectfully, but they should not override her autonomy or access to appropriate pain management.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of a family support system for a pregnant woman in Ghana?

choices.text: A relative who helps arrange transport for antenatal appointments
A stranger who prevents her from attending antenatal clinic
A neighbour who discourages her from reporting danger signs
A family member who withholds essential pregnancy information

questions.rationale: Family support systems provide practical, emotional, financial or informational assistance. Arranging transport for antenatal care is a practical form of support that can improve access to maternal health services.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman is cared for by her grandmother because her parents work in another region. Which term best describes this arrangement?

choices.text: Nuclear family care
Kinship care
Institutional care
Peer supervision

questions.rationale: Kinship care refers to care provided by relatives or members of the extended family. In Ghana, grandparents and other relatives may play important roles in supporting pregnant women and young mothers.

questions.question_text: A woman in a polygynous household reports that she receives little support from her husband because his financial responsibilities are shared among several households. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Assume that all polygynous families provide inadequate support
Assess her actual financial, emotional and practical support needs without making assumptions about the family structure
Tell her that she must leave the household before receiving care
Discuss her situation with other wives without her permission

questions.rationale: Polygyny is a family structure in which a man has more than one wife, but the level of support varies between households. Individual assessment helps the midwife identify the woman's actual needs without stereotyping her family.

questions.question_text: A woman has no partner or close relatives living nearby but has supportive neighbours and a community health nurse. How should the midwife use this information?

choices.text: Classify the woman as having no possible support system
Develop a support plan that includes appropriate community resources and trusted contacts chosen by the woman
Require her to identify a husband before receiving maternity care
Exclude community health workers from her care plan

questions.rationale: Support systems can include trusted neighbours, community health workers and other community resources, not only biological relatives or partners. The midwife should identify safe and acceptable sources of support with the woman's involvement.

questions.question_text: A woman with limited family support is at risk of missing antenatal appointments because she cannot afford transport. Which intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Label her as non-compliant and discontinue follow-up
Explore available community resources, referral options and practical transport arrangements with her
Advise her to attend only when she develops symptoms
Ask her to borrow money without assessing other options

questions.rationale: Financial and transport barriers can prevent timely access to essential maternity services. The midwife should identify practical solutions and appropriate community support rather than blaming the woman.

questions.question_text: During a family assessment, a midwife discovers that a woman's relatives are supportive but strongly discourage facility delivery because of a previous negative experience. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Dismiss the family's concerns and end the discussion
Listen to their experience, address specific concerns and explain available maternity services and emergency referral arrangements
Promise that complications can never occur at the facility
Tell the woman to hide her birth plan from her relatives

questions.rationale: Understanding the family's concerns can help the midwife address barriers to facility-based maternity care. Accurate information and respectful discussion can support informed birth planning without making unrealistic guarantees.

questions.question_text: Which is a potential benefit of appropriate partner involvement in antenatal care?

choices.text: It transfers the woman's right to make healthcare decisions to her partner
It can improve emotional support, birth preparedness and recognition of pregnancy danger signs
It eliminates the need for professional antenatal assessment
It guarantees an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery

questions.rationale: Supportive partner involvement can strengthen emotional support and help couples prepare for childbirth and emergencies. It should complement professional care and preserve the woman's autonomy.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman attends antenatal clinic with her partner, who answers every question on her behalf. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Direct all questions to the partner because he accompanied her
Address the woman directly and offer an opportunity for private discussion
Assume that the partner's answers are always accurate
Ask the partner to sign consent forms for all procedures

questions.rationale: The pregnant woman is the primary recipient of maternity care and should have the opportunity to communicate her own concerns. Private discussion also supports confidentiality and helps identify possible coercion or safety concerns.

questions.question_text: During antenatal education, a midwife teaches a woman's partner how to recognise danger signs such as vaginal bleeding, severe headache and convulsions. What is the main purpose of this education?

choices.text: To make the partner responsible for diagnosing obstetric complications
To enable the partner to recognise warning signs and support prompt access to emergency care
To allow the partner to decide whether professional treatment is necessary
To replace the woman's need for antenatal follow-up

questions.rationale: A knowledgeable partner may help identify danger signs and facilitate timely referral to a health facility. Recognition and support do not make the partner responsible for clinical diagnosis or treatment.

questions.question_text: A woman tells the midwife that she does not want her partner involved in her antenatal consultations. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Refuse her request because partner involvement is compulsory
Respect her preference and provide confidential care, while exploring any concerns she wishes to discuss
Inform the partner that the woman has refused his involvement
Delay her antenatal care until the partner attends

questions.rationale: Partner involvement should be voluntary and guided by the woman's wishes. Confidential maternity care must not be withheld because a woman chooses not to involve her partner.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman and her partner are preparing for childbirth. Which action best demonstrates effective birth preparedness?

choices.text: Waiting until labour begins before deciding where to deliver
Identifying the intended delivery facility, transport arrangements, emergency contacts and available resources
Relying entirely on neighbours to identify complications
Avoiding discussion of possible emergencies to prevent anxiety

questions.rationale: Birth preparedness involves planning for normal delivery and possible complications before labour begins. Identifying a facility, transport and emergency contacts can reduce delays in accessing skilled care.

questions.question_text: A woman's partner refuses permission for her to receive an urgent referral for suspected severe pre-eclampsia. The woman is conscious and agrees to the referral. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Cancel the referral because the partner has refused
Respect the woman's informed decision, explain the urgency and arrange appropriate emergency referral
Wait for a family meeting before taking any action
Ask the partner to sign a refusal form on the woman's behalf

questions.rationale: A woman with decision-making capacity has the right to make decisions about her own healthcare. Suspected severe pre-eclampsia requires urgent assessment and management, and a partner's refusal does not override the woman's informed decision.

questions.question_text: A midwife is assessing a family in which the pregnant woman is financially dependent on her husband, has limited contact with relatives and reports frequent arguments at home. Which assessment approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Focus only on the husband's income because financial status is the main determinant of family health
Assess the woman's emotional wellbeing, safety, relationships, practical support and access to resources, including privately where appropriate
Conclude that the family is dysfunctional without further assessment
Ask the husband to complete the assessment without the woman's involvement

questions.rationale: A comprehensive family assessment considers physical, emotional, social and economic factors rather than focusing on one issue. Private assessment is important where relationship conflict or possible coercion may affect the woman's safety and autonomy.

questions.question_text: A woman who has experienced a previous traumatic birth becomes anxious when the midwife discusses her current birth plan. Which communication approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Tell her that the previous experience is irrelevant to the current pregnancy
Use a trauma-informed approach, acknowledge her experience and ask what would help her feel safe during care
Avoid discussing the birth plan until labour begins
Tell her that all women experience childbirth in the same way

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed communication recognises the possible effects of previous distressing experiences and seeks to promote safety, trust and choice. It allows the woman to express concerns and participate in planning care that respects her preferences.

questions.question_text: A woman is unable to read a consent form and appears uncertain about a proposed procedure. What should the midwife do before proceeding?

choices.text: Ask her to make a mark on the form without further explanation
Explain the procedure in an understandable way, check her understanding and ensure that her decision is voluntary
Obtain consent from another patient who can read
Assume that her attendance at the facility means she has consented

questions.rationale: Inability to read does not remove a woman's right to informed consent. The midwife should provide an accessible explanation, check understanding and follow appropriate procedures for documenting consent.

questions.question_text: During a home visit, a woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy reports that she has not felt fetal movements as usual since the previous evening. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Reassure her that reduced fetal movement is normal in late pregnancy
Arrange prompt assessment at a health facility for reduced fetal movements
Advise her to wait until her next routine antenatal appointment
Recommend that she drink a sugary beverage and ignore the symptoms if movement briefly returns

questions.rationale: A reduction or change in the usual pattern of fetal movements requires prompt assessment. The midwife should not delay referral by relying on home remedies or routine follow-up.

questions.question_text: A woman in the postnatal ward is having difficulty breastfeeding. Her mother-in-law repeatedly criticises her and insists on giving the newborn water. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Allow the mother-in-law to decide because she has more childcare experience
Assess the breastfeeding difficulty, support the mother and respectfully explain appropriate exclusive breastfeeding practices
Tell the woman to stop breastfeeding until her family agrees
Exclude the woman from all newborn-care discussions

questions.rationale: The midwife should assess the breastfeeding problem and provide practical support to the mother. Family education can address misconceptions while preserving the mother's role in decisions about newborn feeding.

questions.question_text: A woman requests that a cultural naming practice be performed after delivery. The practice can be safely accommodated without interfering with essential newborn care. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Automatically prohibit the practice because it is not a clinical procedure
Support the practice where feasible while ensuring that essential maternal and newborn care is maintained
Allow the practice to delay emergency treatment if a complication develops
Require the woman to abandon all cultural practices during the postnatal period

questions.rationale: Safe cultural practices can be accommodated as part of respectful maternity care. The midwife must ensure that essential interventions, newborn protection and timely treatment of complications are not compromised.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman identifies her older sister as the person she trusts most to support her during labour. Her husband is not available because he works outside the region. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Reject the sister because only husbands can be birth companions
Discuss the woman's preference and facilitate the sister's involvement where appropriate
Require the woman to wait until her husband returns before making a birth plan
Assume that the woman has no support because her husband is absent

questions.rationale: Support can come from any trusted person chosen by the woman, including a sister or other relative. The midwife should assess the woman's preferences and facilitate appropriate support without making assumptions about family roles.

questions.question_text: A partner attends antenatal clinic and asks to know the woman's HIV test result. The woman has not given permission to share it. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Disclose the result because the partner accompanied the woman
Maintain confidentiality and discuss disclosure with the woman in accordance with applicable guidelines
Give the partner a copy of the woman's entire clinical record
Ask other patients to persuade the woman to disclose her result

questions.rationale: A partner's attendance does not automatically authorise access to confidential health information. The midwife must protect the woman's privacy and follow applicable HIV testing, counselling and disclosure guidelines.

questions.question_text: A midwife uses a genogram to document that a woman's mother had twins and that two maternal aunts also had twin pregnancies. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: The woman will certainly have twins
The family history may be relevant to assessing the possibility of multiple pregnancy, but it does not confirm one
The woman does not need an ultrasound assessment
The genogram establishes the gestational age of the current pregnancy

questions.rationale: A family history of twinning may be relevant, particularly where there is a history of spontaneous fraternal twinning. However, a genogram cannot confirm multiple pregnancy, which requires appropriate clinical assessment and ultrasound where indicated.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman lives in a crowded compound house with several relatives. She reports that she has no private place to sleep and is frequently exposed to cigarette smoke. Which response best demonstrates comprehensive family assessment?

choices.text: Focus only on the number of people in the household
Assess the effects of overcrowding and smoke exposure, explore feasible household changes and provide appropriate health education
Tell her to leave the household immediately without assessing her circumstances
Ignore the living environment because it is not part of antenatal care

questions.rationale: The home environment can affect maternal health, comfort and exposure to health risks. A comprehensive assessment identifies these concerns and works with the woman and family to develop realistic risk-reduction measures.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour requests an explanation before an emergency procedure, but her condition is deteriorating and immediate intervention may be necessary. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Ignore her completely because emergencies remove all patient rights
Provide a brief, clear explanation and obtain consent where feasible without causing a dangerous delay, following emergency and legal protocols
Wait indefinitely until every relative has arrived
Allow a non-clinical relative to decide whether the procedure is necessary

questions.rationale: Emergency care should respect the woman's autonomy and provide understandable information whenever feasible. If she lacks capacity and urgent treatment is required, the team should follow applicable legal and professional emergency-care protocols while avoiding harmful delay.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman says, 'My partner does not support this pregnancy, and I feel alone.' Which response best demonstrates empathy?

choices.text: You should have thought about that before becoming pregnant
At least you have a baby to look forward to
It sounds as though you are feeling unsupported. Would you like to tell me more about what has been happening?
You must convince your partner to attend the next clinic visit

questions.rationale: The response acknowledges the woman's feelings and invites her to share more without judgement. Empathy helps establish trust and allows the midwife to assess emotional and practical support needs.

questions.question_text: A community midwife plans visits to several pregnant women in a rural area. Which woman should receive the earliest urgent assessment or referral?

choices.text: A woman at 20 weeks with no complaints who attended her scheduled antenatal appointment
A woman at 36 weeks with severe headache, visual disturbance and facial swelling
A woman at 24 weeks requesting information about breastfeeding
A woman at 18 weeks asking about suitable exercise during pregnancy

questions.rationale: Severe headache and visual disturbance in pregnancy may indicate severe pre-eclampsia, which can rapidly become life-threatening. This woman requires urgent assessment and referral ahead of routine health education or follow-up visits.

questions.question_text: A woman with a newborn who requires specialised care is distressed because she believes that separation means she cannot participate in her baby's care. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Tell her that newborn care is exclusively the responsibility of neonatal staff
Explain the newborn's care needs and identify safe opportunities for her involvement, including feeding, touch and communication where clinically appropriate
Discourage her from asking questions about the newborn
Promise that the newborn will be discharged immediately

questions.rationale: Family-centred care recognises parents as important participants in the care of their newborn, even when specialised treatment is required. Clear communication and safe involvement can reduce distress and support bonding.

questions.question_text: A woman explains that her family expects her to consume a traditional herbal preparation during pregnancy. She is unsure whether it is safe. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Assure her that all traditional preparations are safe because they are natural
Ask about the preparation and its ingredients where known, assess possible risks and advise her to avoid unverified substances pending appropriate clinical guidance
Tell her to conceal the preparation from other healthcare workers
Recommend a different herbal preparation without assessing its safety

questions.rationale: Natural or traditional products are not automatically safe during pregnancy, and some may have harmful or unknown effects. A respectful discussion allows the midwife to assess exposure and provide evidence-informed advice without dismissing the woman's cultural background.

questions.question_text: A midwife notices that a partner answers questions for the woman, controls her NHIS card and refuses to let her speak privately. The woman appears distressed. What is the most appropriate next action?

choices.text: Continue the consultation with the partner because he controls the household documents
Arrange a safe private conversation with the woman, assess possible coercion or abuse and follow appropriate safeguarding procedures
Confront the partner publicly and accuse him of abuse
Discharge the woman because the partner is interfering with care

questions.rationale: Controlling access to healthcare documents and preventing private communication may indicate coercive control or abuse. The midwife should assess the woman's safety confidentially and follow appropriate safeguarding and referral procedures without increasing her risk.
